title: Prime Loop Till sqrt(n)
statement:
A **prime number** is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. You are given `t` integers. For each one, decide whether it is prime.

The numbers can be as large as 10^10, so testing every possible divisor up to `n` is far too slow. A prime check only needs to try divisors up to `sqrt(n)`.

**Follow-up:** the interviewer first asked how many primes are below 10 (there are four: 2, 3, 5 and 7), then asked for prime-checking code, then asked why the loop only needs to run up to `Math.sqrt(n)`, and finally what the Big O of the check is. Be ready to explain these.
input_format:
The first line contains an integer `t`.
The second line contains `t` integers `n_1 ... n_t`.
output_format: Print `t` lines. Line `i` is `YES` if `n_i` is prime and `NO` otherwise.

examples.explanation: 2 and 97 have no divisors besides 1 and themselves. 9 = 3 × 3 and 100 = 10 × 10 are composite. 1 is not prime by definition.
7 is prime. 8 is divisible by 2. 49 = 7 × 7, and 7 is exactly sqrt(49), which shows the loop bound must include sqrt(n).

hints: If n = a × b with a ≤ b, then a ≤ sqrt(n). So if there is any divisor, there is one that is at most sqrt(n).
Handle n < 2 separately, then try divisors from 2 while `d * d <= n`. Use integer arithmetic, not floating-point sqrt, to avoid rounding errors.
You can skip even candidates after checking 2 to halve the work.
brute:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
t = int(data[0])
out = []
for x in data[1:1 + t]:
    n = int(x)
    ok = n >= 2
    for d in range(2, n):
        if n % d == 0:
            ok = False
            break
    out.append('YES' if ok else 'NO')
print('\n'.join(out))
